node.label: Peter Burke
node.date_label: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978) · The French Historical Revolution: The Annales School, 1929–89 (1990) · What is Cultural History? (2004)
node.description: A cultural historian of early modern Europe who also writes about historical methods and the history of knowledge. His selected historiographical essay resists describing cultural history as a simple sequence in which each approach displaces the last. In a 2022 interview, he explains how Popular Culture combined wide comparison with attention to regional variation and discusses how changing scale alters historical explanation. The interview also insists on multiple historical voices, connecting structures with individual experience rather than choosing one for every inquiry.

incident_edges.relationship: Questions a simple replacement model of cultural approaches while investigating historical meanings and cultural variation.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Reuse of the existing essay reading, PDF pp. 1–13 and selected opening of p. 14. The arrow adopts its limited anti-succession argument, not all of Burke’s survey or a verified genealogy for every predecessor.

incident_edges.relationship: Explains how changes in research scale alter plausible explanations, linking regional cultural variation with wider comparisons.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary interview, question 7, read. Burke discusses the scale question and describes his own popular-culture research; this is a methodological contribution, not membership in one microhistorical school or a claim that he invented scale analysis.

incident_edges.relationship: Armitage credits Burke’s formative questions and support for a seminar connecting cultural and intellectual history with colonial encounters.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2000 acknowledgment credits Burke with Bayly,Collinson,Hont and Pagden;own2012 account specifies support for Cultural Encounters in the Early-Modern World,which Armitage organized with Joan-Pau Rubiés. Neither sole supervision nor a particular question is inferred.

incident_edges.relationship: Questions Mosse’s emphasis on festivals and broad trends by contrasting it with attention to everyday practice, particular events and varied audience meanings.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Burke’s own874–875 identifies two differences and asks what a more detailed performance approach could add, while also asking later ethnographers to learn from Mosse’s broad analysis. The criticism is qualified and retrospective: it does not claim those later writers directly refuted Mosse or that he could have read work published after his death. Original monographs remain unread here.

incident_edges.relationship: Provides Burke with a central account of secular liturgy and political symbolism for reassessing the history of cultural and performance approaches.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Burke865/868 takes Nationalization of the Masses as a specific reference point for studying ritual and later performance, and876–877 credits its transformation of modern political history. This is analytical use in Burke’s own historiographical argument, not merely a publisher’s praise, formal mentoring or agreement with all Mosse conclusions. Burke’s qualification is separately represented.

named_group_routes.relationship: provides an earlier cultural tradition that later work transforms
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Burckhardt and Huizinga are earlier resources; later cultural histories change subject matter, social reach, and method. Burke’s selective account explicitly rejects a simple succession of superior methods and describes the continuing German cultural-history tradition alongside alternatives; it is not a complete transmission chain for every later historian.

named_group_routes.relationship: Armitage credits Pagden with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral study that developed into The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Armitage’s own acknowledgments p. x explicitly group Pagden with Chris Bayly, Peter Burke, Patrick Collinson and Istvan Hont in this Cambridge phase. All retain credit. This supports the named research contribution, not sole supervision, a particular question whose wording is unknown, or an inference from first meeting or institutional membership. Selected acknowledgments and publication leaves were read; Armitage’s full monograph remains unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Armitage credits Bayly with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral research that became The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.

named_group_routes.relationship: Armitage and Guldi use Levi’s account of microhistory’s transformative capacity to qualify their criticism of its later anglophone practice.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Joint2014 quotation and attribution retain individual agency within constraining normative systems. This does not make Levi responsible for the book’s diagnosis of anglophone microhistory or identify him with the later practice criticized. His1991 chapter remains unread;Peter Burke is volume editor.

named_group_routes.relationship: Brewer uses Ginzburg’s account of clues, constructed research and incomplete historical truth to explain microhistory’s humanist realism.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own2010 uses cited1989 Clues96–125,1993 Microhistory23–24/27/32–33 and Wooden Eyes2001p156; John/Anne C.Tedeschi translation credit retained for Clues and the1993 English essay; Wooden Eyes is translated by Martin Ryle and Kate Soper. Kracauer and Pallares-Burke remain explicit intermediaries where cited. Constructed interpretation is not equated with fiction or completeness; original works unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Brewer uses Levi’s account of scale and negotiated agency to explain what microhistorical inquiry can reveal.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own2010 distinguishes methodological shifts of observation from narrative completeness. Cited On Microhistory in Peter Burke ed.(1991)94–98/106/110 and Origins of the Modern State(1998)58–62 are reader locators, not fresh originals. The same essay’s specific reservation is separately retained.

named_group_routes.relationship: Cites Lévi-Strauss while arguing for a historical anthropology of mass movements, as Burke identifies.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Burke’s2021 discussion868/n14 explicitly identifies Mosse’s1969 review article as citing Franz Boas and Lévi-Strauss in its argument. This is a bounded named scholarly account of an anthropological resource, not a claim of direct training, complete structuralism or an independently read original article. Boas retains credit; exact Lévi-Strauss title is not invented.

named_group_routes.relationship: Disagrees with the invention-of-tradition approach despite sharing its interest in national ritual, as Burke reports through Moro.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Burke869 expressly reports Mosse’s disagreement and cites Renato Moro’s2014 chapter131–136 in note20. This two-stage scholarly mediation is explicit; original Mosse statement and Moro chapter unread. Hobsbawm’s coeditor Terence Ranger retains credit, and lack of autobiography references is not treated as proof of hostility or an intellectual debt. No general rejection of every Hobsbawm work.

named_group_routes.relationship: Burke places Mosse alongside new cultural historians in their converging attention to ritual, representation, memory, gender and the body.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Burke865 explicitly describes different starting points and later converging interests, naming Davis, Thomas Laqueur and Hunt. This attributed comparison establishes no teacher-pupil relation or direction of influence. Thomas Laqueur retains credit despite lacking a graph endpoint; he is not Walter Laqueur. Original works of the compared historians remain unread for this dossier.
